sections.plainEnglish:
To test a self-service tool, act like the user. Sign in as a normal pilot user, set up recovery information, and then try the reset website. Use a private browser window so your administrator session does not get mixed into the test. Do not use an administrator account because administrators have stricter recovery rules that employees may not see.

Registration and reset are not the same test. Registration proves the user can set up recovery information. Reset proves the user can use that information when locked out. A good pilot checks both steps, because many failed rollouts happen when users are told SSPR is enabled but have not registered enough methods.

Testing as an ordinary pilot user also finds communication problems. If the user does not understand the prompt, cannot access a phone, or sees a missing method, you discover that before the feature is announced to everyone.
sections.analogy:
A store tests self-checkout by having someone buy an item like a normal customer, not by using the manager override screen.

| Analogy | Azure reality |
|---|---|
| Normal customer | Non-admin pilot user |
| Self-checkout setup | `aka.ms/ssprsetup` |
| Self-checkout purchase | `aka.ms/sspr` reset |
| Manager override | Admin reset policy |

**Where the analogy breaks down:** Browser tokens and Microsoft Entra policies are more complex than a checkout lane.

jargon.definition: Self-service password reset, a feature for users to reset or change passwords after verifying identity.
A private browser mode that avoids using an existing signed-in session.
The process of saving authentication information for later password reset or MFA use.
A highly privileged Microsoft Entra administrator role.
Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure Active Directory.
A challenge used to reduce automated abuse by asking for proof that a human is using the form.
Browser and identity data that can keep a user signed in across pages or tabs.

sections.watchOut:
- Register methods before testing reset.
- Use non-admin accounts for regular SSPR validation.
- Private browsing prevents testing the wrong cached account.
- Admin-initiated reset does not prove self-service reset works.
- `aka.ms/ssprsetup` and `aka.ms/sspr` test different parts of the journey.
- Existing browser sessions can hide prompts or use the wrong account.
- A user outside the selected SSPR group can register some methods but still fail reset eligibility.
- Hybrid tests should include writeback validation, not only the cloud portal success page.

productionTip.official: Microsoft's SSPR tutorial lists a non-administrator user as a prerequisite and uses `aka.ms/ssprsetup` for registration followed by `aka.ms/sspr` for password reset testing. The tutorial's test section explicitly uses a non-administrator test user in a selected group and instructs the tester to browse first to the setup portal and then to the password reset portal.
productionTip.recommendation: Create a pilot test script that checks scope, registration, reset, notifications, and writeback if hybrid users are included. Use the same script for help desk training. After a successful pilot reset, sign in with the new password to a representative application and, for hybrid users, verify on-premises access or expected writeback behavior. Record exact screens and error messages for support documentation.

sections.memoryTrick: Test SSPR with the same kind of user who will use SSPR. Use admin accounts only when testing admin recovery.
sections.examTip: Clue words are **end-user**, **pilot group**, and **not affected by administrator policy**. The answer must use a non-admin account and the SSPR setup and reset portals. A harder version may include a user outside the selected group; registration does not make that user eligible if scope is wrong. Rule out administrator accounts for employee validation because their reset policy is stricter. Rule out admin-center resets because they skip the user's self-service path. A harder version may ask why a test user reaches setup but cannot reset; likely causes include not being in SSPR scope, too few methods, or missing writeback for a synchronized account.

sources.title: Enable Microsoft Entra self-service password reset

prompt:
Your organization synchronized `mobile` and `telephoneNumber` values from AD DS to Microsoft Entra ID for years. Many users never completed SSPR registration in Security info. After October 5, 2026, some users report that SSPR no longer accepts their directory-sourced phone data for verification.

What should you do?

options.text: Tell users to keep relying on `mobilePhone`, `businessPhone`, and `otherMails` because directory-sourced values are always accepted
Disable combined registration because only legacy registration accepts phone numbers
Require affected users to explicitly register enough authentication methods that satisfy the SSPR policy, and monitor users who still lack required methods
Set reconfirmation to `0` days so Microsoft Entra trusts synchronized directory values again

assumptions: Azure public cloud. The organization is following current Microsoft documentation verified in October 2026. Users are regular users, not administrators.

sections.correctAnswer: **C. Require affected users to explicitly register enough authentication methods that satisfy the SSPR policy, and monitor users who still lack required methods**. Microsoft documents that starting October 5, 2026, SSPR accepts only explicitly registered methods, not unregistered directory-sourced profile values.
sections.technical:
Prepopulated contact information historically helped bootstrap SSPR. Microsoft documents default Microsoft Entra Connect mappings such as `telephoneNumber` to Office phone and `mobile` to Mobile phone. Current documentation adds important 2026 changes. Starting October 5, 2026, SSPR only accepts explicitly registered authentication methods. Directory-sourced properties such as `mobilePhone`, `businessPhone`, and `otherMails` that were never registered no longer work for SSPR verification. Starting November 9, 2026, if SSPR settings require registration during sign-in and enabled users do not have enough methods to complete SSPR, a registration campaign prompts affected users to register methods ahead of enforcement. The fix is explicit method registration that satisfies the SSPR method count and allowed-method policy.

The current rule changes the meaning of prepopulation. Synchronized phone and email attributes can still help users see familiar values during registration, and administrators can still review certain user authentication information with the appropriate role. But for SSPR verification after the documented date, the service requires methods that are explicitly registered for authentication. A stale `mobile` value copied from AD DS is not enough by itself.

Scope and method count still apply after explicit registration. If the tenant requires two methods, a user who registers only one phone method remains below the reset requirement. If phone methods are enabled but the user's number is badly formatted, the method may not be usable. Microsoft documents phone number format requirements such as including the country code and a space before the phone number for prepopulated phone data. These details turn this from a one-time directory cleanup into a real registration and validation project.

wrongOptions.A: Current Microsoft documentation says unregistered directory-sourced values no longer work for SSPR verification after the date. Misconception: profile attributes and registered security methods are equivalent forever. Could be correct when: describing historical behavior or profile display only A historical scenario before the documented change could have relied more heavily on prepopulated values, which is why this distractor sounds plausible to experienced administrators.
wrongOptions.B: Combined registration is the current security info experience, not the cause of the documented requirement. Misconception: new registration experiences broke phone methods. Could be correct when: a separate documented service issue requires a temporary registration workaround
wrongOptions.D: `0` means never reconfirm; it does not make unregistered values trusted again. Misconception: reconfirmation controls acceptance of directory attributes. Could be correct when: the goal is to stop periodic reconfirmation prompts

sections.plainEnglish:
A phone number in a company directory is not the same as a phone number registered as a security method. Microsoft now requires SSPR verification to use explicitly registered methods. If a user never completed Security info registration, their synced work phone may appear on the profile but still not count for reset. Have users register valid methods and verify that they have enough methods for your SSPR policy.

The old directory phone number is like a contact printed on an employee record. The registered security method is like the employee saying, “Use this phone for account recovery,” and completing the setup process. Microsoft's newer rule trusts the second kind for SSPR verification.

Therefore the fix is not just to clean up AD fields. Cleaning up AD may still be useful, but users must go through Security info registration or another supported registration process so Microsoft Entra has recovery methods recorded as authentication methods. Then the organization must check that users have the right number of methods for the policy.
sections.analogy:
A school has parent phone numbers in its student system, but pickups now require an approved pickup contact. A number in the old record is not enough unless registered for pickup.

| Analogy | Azure reality |
|---|---|
| Student system phone | Directory-sourced property |
| Approved pickup contact | Explicitly registered method |
| Two contacts required | Two-method SSPR policy |
| Reminder campaign | Registration campaign |

**Where the analogy breaks down:** Microsoft Entra stores method objects and evaluates policy during reset; a school record system is less automated.

jargon.definition: A user profile value synchronized from a directory, such as phone or email.
An authentication method registered for security verification, not merely a directory profile attribute.
The user page for managing authentication methods.
The process of saving authentication information for later password reset or MFA use.
Self-service password reset, a feature for users to reset or change passwords after verifying identity.
A synchronization tool between AD DS and Microsoft Entra ID.
A registered proof option such as phone, app, email, or other supported factor.
The required way to store a phone number, such as including country code and spacing, so verification systems can use it.

sections.watchOut:
- October 5, 2026 is the key date in the fetched Microsoft documentation.
- Profile phone data can exist without satisfying SSPR verification.
- If two methods are required, one registered phone is insufficient.
- Phone formatting still matters when registering phone methods.
- Directory cleanup alone does not equal explicit SSPR method registration.
- A registration campaign helps only users who are in scope and subject to the configured registration conditions.
- `0` reconfirmation stops scheduled review; it does not preserve old prepopulation behavior.
- Bad phone formatting can still undermine a phone-based rollout.

productionTip.official: Microsoft's prepopulation documentation states that starting October 5, 2026, SSPR only accepts explicitly registered methods and that a registration campaign begins November 9, 2026 for enabled users lacking enough methods when registration is required. The same prepopulation article maps `telephoneNumber` to Office phone and `mobile` to Mobile phone under default Microsoft Entra Connect settings, while separately warning that unregistered directory-sourced values stop working for SSPR verification.
productionTip.recommendation: Identify users relying only on directory-sourced values and guide them through Security info registration. Do not assume HR or AD phone fields are valid recovery methods unless explicitly registered. Segment reports into users with no registered methods, users with one method when two are required, and users whose registered methods are weak or phone-only. Use targeted communications rather than a generic tenant-wide email, because the remediation differs by registration state.

sections.memoryTrick: A profile phone is not a proof phone unless it is registered. This shortcut allows that profile data may still be visible but not accepted for reset verification.
sections.examTip: Clue words are **after October 5, 2026**, **directory-sourced**, and **never completed registration**. The answer is explicit method registration, not changing reconfirmation or disabling combined registration. A harder version may ask about November 9, 2026 and the registration campaign for users lacking methods. Rule out answers that say synchronized profile values are always enough; the date in the prompt is the giveaway. Rule out reconfirmation changes because they affect review prompts, not whether a property counts as an authentication method. A harder version may ask how to prepare before November 9, 2026; enable registration during sign-in and monitor the campaign for users lacking enough methods.
